Rerankers &Hybrid Search

Why vector search alone misses things, what a cross-encoder fixes, and how to add a keyword channel so retrieval can do both meaning and exact-match.

RAG PART 2 LANGCHAIN · BGE · FAISS · BM25
The bi-encoder retriever is the cheap, broad first pass. The cross-encoder reranker is the expensive, precise second pass. You almost always want both.
Where we are. Session 12 built the indexing half of RAG (load → chunk → embed → store). Session 13 wired retrieval into a basic LCEL chain — but the document set was never actually indexed in that live run, so retrievals came back empty. Session 14 fixes that, then layers two upgrades on top of plain vector retrieval: a reranker that re-scores the top candidates, and hybrid search (vector + BM25) that widens what gets considered in the first place.
§ 01 — THE PROBLEM

The pipeline so far, and what's still wrong with it

The retrieval step is just a vector search: embed the question, find the k chunks whose embeddings are closest to it (cosine / L2 distance), feed those into the prompt. That is fast. It is also shallow, in three ways:

  1. The question and each chunk are embedded independently by the same model. Their vectors are produced without ever "seeing" each other. The similarity score is computed after both vectors exist. This architecture is called a bi-encoder (two encoders, or the same encoder applied twice).
  2. Multi-hop / reasoning questions where the answer is assembled from several sections may not match any single chunk strongly. The right chunks individually look "topical but not directly on point" — and get outranked by chunks that share more surface words.
  3. k is fixed. If you ask for k=10, you get 10 chunks, even if only 3 are relevant. The other 7 dilute the context and increase the chance the LLM grounds its answer in noise.

Vector search optimizes for speed and recall. It does not optimize for precision — which of the candidates actually answers the question.

JAVA / SPRING BRIDGE

Vector retrieval is like running a LIKE query against a precomputed full-text index — fast, broad, lossy. You usually wouldn't ship that result straight to the caller; you'd post-filter and re-rank on the application layer. A reranker is exactly that post-filter.

§ 02 — RERANKERS

What a reranker does, and why it's needed

A reranker is a second-stage model that re-scores the top candidates from the first-stage retriever. Instead of comparing two precomputed vectors with cosine distance, it takes the query and one candidate chunk as a single joined input, runs a transformer over them together, and outputs a single scalar relevance score.

StageJobModelSpeedInputs
1 — Retriever (bi-encoder)Cheap recall over many docsBi-encoder embedding (BGE, OpenAI, …)Fast — vectors precomputed at index timeQuery & chunk separately
2 — Reranker (cross-encoder)Precise scoring of a few candidatesCross-encoder (e.g. ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2)Slow — one forward pass per candidate, at query timeQuery & chunk together

The standard pattern is retrieve-then-rerank: fetch a generous candidate set (say k=10 or k=20) with the bi-encoder, then rerank that small list with the cross-encoder, then keep the top 3–5 for the prompt.

WHY IT HELPS

When a transformer sees query and document tokens in the same sequence, self-attention can compute term-level interactions: "the word deep in the query is supported by the phrase layers of neural networks in the document." A bi-encoder, by design, never gets that chance — each side is compressed to a single vector before the comparison.

The lecturer phrased the trade-off as a hiring rule of thumb: "reranker is compulsory; hybrid search is optional." That is his preference, not a law — but for any retrieval over policy documents, contracts, or other paragraph-style prose, reranking usually earns its latency.

Drop-by-score, not just reorder

A reranker can do more than reorder. It can also drop candidates whose relevance score falls below a threshold. If vector search returned 10 chunks and the cross-encoder scores 7 of them under 0.2, you keep only the top 3. The prompt gets shorter, cheaper, and less noisy — which is itself a quality improvement.

§ 03 — THE ARCHITECTURAL DIFFERENCE

Bi-encoder vs cross-encoder

Both use the same transformer encoder architecture. The difference is what gets fed in.

  • One transformer pass, joined input. The cross-encoder sees the query and the document as one token sequence. Self-attention can directly compute interactions between query tokens and document tokens.
  • The output is a scalar, not a vector. A small linear layer reads the final hidden state of the [CLS] token (the first special token in BERT-family models) and projects it to a single relevance score, typically passed through a sigmoid to land in [0, 1].
  • Nothing is precomputed. Every (query, candidate) pair needs its own forward pass at query time. That's why you only rerank a short list — cross-encoder scoring over a million chunks is not viable in a real-time chatbot.
NAMING COLLISION WORTH KNOWING

The "cross-encoder" of reranking literature is unrelated to the encoder-decoder cross-attention inside the original Transformer paper (Vaswani et al. 2017), even though both have "cross" in their names. Cross-attention is a mechanism (the decoder attending to encoder outputs). A cross-encoder is an architecture choice (concatenate two inputs and feed them through a single encoder). If you see the term in a paper, it's almost always the IR sense.

ORIGIN

Bi-encoder vs. cross-encoder terminology, in its modern reranking form, was popularized by Reimers & Gurevych, Sentence-BERT (EMNLP 2019). The canonical cross-encoder reranker for passage retrieval is Nogueira & Cho, Passage Re-ranking with BERT (2019), known as monoBERT.

§ 04 — HYBRID SEARCH

Adding a keyword channel — BM25

Vector search captures meaning. "Puppy" matches "dog." But it sometimes loses on exact terms: model numbers, acronyms, names, billing codes. A query that hinges on the literal token "Modifier 54" can be outranked by chunks that are semantically about billing but never use that string.

The fix is to run a second retriever in parallel that uses lexical matching, and combine the two ranked lists.

BM25 in one paragraph

BM25 (Best Matching 25, Robertson & Walker, Okapi system, 1995 — the "25" is the iteration number) is the standard keyword-ranking algorithm. It scores a document for a query by summing a per-term contribution: how often each query term appears in the document (term frequency), weighted by how rare that term is across the corpus (inverse document frequency), with two adjustments — term saturation (the 50th occurrence of "the" doesn't help more than the 5th) and document-length normalization (long documents don't get an automatic advantage). It is the descendant of TF-IDF that production search engines have used for decades.

VECTOR · WHAT IT GETS RIGHT

Semantic

  • + synonyms / paraphrase
  • + "puppy" ≈ "dog"
  • + phrasing variance
  • − exact codes / IDs
  • − rare acronyms
BM25 · WHAT IT GETS RIGHT

Lexical

  • + exact tokens
  • + acronyms, codes, names
  • + rare technical terms
  • − synonyms
  • − no word-order / syntax

That's why hybrid is "vector + BM25," not "BM25 instead." They have complementary failure modes.

§ 05 — FUSION

Reciprocal Rank Fusion

Two retrievers return two ranked lists. How do you merge them? The standard answer is Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) (Cormack, Clarke, Büttcher, SIGIR 2009). For each document d, sum its reciprocal-rank score across the source rankings:

RRF(d) = Σ_i  1 / (k + rank_i(d))

where rank_i(d) is d's position in the i-th ranked list (1 = top) and k is a smoothing constant (the paper recommends k = 60, which is also LangChain's default in EnsembleRetriever).

A CONFUSING NAME COLLISION

Two unrelated things in RAG land are both called "k": k in retrieval means "give me the top k results" (e.g. k=4). k in the RRF formula is a smoothing constant (usually 60) that controls how much a top-rank result outweighs a mid-rank one. They are unrelated — read the surrounding context.

Worked example with k = 1 (what the lecturer drew on the board)

To keep the arithmetic easy, the lecturer set the smoothing constant to 1, not 60. Relative ordering is the same; only the numbers change.

When hybrid helps, when it doesn't

The lecturer's rule of thumb: "vector search is good for semantic search; BM25 catches the exact terms vector search misses. Sometimes hybrid wins, sometimes pure vector wins. You measure." That's honest. Hybrid search is not universally better; it's a layer you try and validate.

A reasonable heuristic: if your corpus has lots of named entities, product codes, version numbers, or acronyms (think technical docs, policy documents, contracts), hybrid is usually worth it. For freeform prose (essays, transcripts), pure vector often suffices.

§ 06 — PUTTING IT TOGETHER

The full pipeline

In LangChain code, this is three composed retrievers:

from langchain_community.retrievers import BM25Retriever
from langchain_classic.retrievers import EnsembleRetriever
from langchain_classic.retrievers.contextual_compression import ContextualCompressionRetriever
from langchain_classic.retrievers.document_compressors import CrossEncoderReranker
from langchain_community.cross_encoders import HuggingFaceCrossEncoder

# 1. Two base retrievers
bm25_ret  = BM25Retriever.from_documents(chunks, k=10)
faiss_ret = vectorstore.as_retriever(search_kwargs={"k": 10})

# 2. Hybrid: fuse them with RRF
hybrid_retriever = EnsembleRetriever(
    retrievers=[faiss_ret, bm25_ret],
    weights=[0.5, 0.5],
)

# 3. Rerank the fused list with a cross-encoder
ce_model   = HuggingFaceCrossEncoder(model_name="cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2")
compressor = CrossEncoderReranker(model=ce_model, top_n=3)

reranked_retriever = ContextualCompressionRetriever(
    base_compressor=compressor,        # what does the re-scoring / dropping
    base_retriever=hybrid_retriever,   # what feeds it candidates
)

The phrase "compression" in ContextualCompressionRetriever is LangChain's term for "shrink the candidate list down to what's actually relevant." Reranking is one form of compression; another is summarizing each chunk. The interface is the same: a BaseDocumentCompressor runs after a base_retriever.

Scope note. The "Complete Guide" notebook in RAG_Project1/ also includes a cell with an alternate cross-encoder compressor class. The lecturer pointed at it but explicitly deferred coding it: "re-ranker, tomorrow we will discuss." The mechanism is identical to the code above; only the wrapper class differs.
§ 07 — RECAP

Indexing + retrieval, worked end-to-end

The lecturer used the "Complete Guide" notebook to revisit the entire Session 12/13 pipeline step by step, this time printing intermediate state so each transition is visible.

Recursive character splitter

text_splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(
    chunk_size=500, chunk_overlap=50,
    separators=["\n\n", "\n", ". ", " ", ""],
)

It tries to split on paragraph breaks first ("\n\n"); if a piece is still over chunk_size, it falls back to single newlines, then sentence boundaries, then spaces, then characters. Actual chunk sizes vary because the splitter prefers natural boundaries over hitting the size target exactly.

Open-source embedding — BGE small

embedding_model = HuggingFaceEmbeddings(
    model_name="BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5",
    model_kwargs={"device": "cpu"},
    encode_kwargs={"normalize_embeddings": True},
)
Correction. BAAI is the Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence, the lab behind the BGE family. The lecturer said "Bayesian Academy of AI" — that's wrong.
  • bge-small-en-v1.5 outputs 384-dimensional vectors. (The lecturer occasionally said "first 20 characters" of the embedding — those are 20 floats, not characters; the embedding is a vector of numbers, not text.)
  • normalize_embeddings=True scales each vector to unit length (Euclidean norm = 1). After normalization, cosine similarity equals a simple dot product, and L2 distance is monotonically related to cosine similarity — ranking by either gives the same order. The "0 to 1" range the lecturer mentioned is loose; the actual property is that vectors lie on the unit sphere.

FAISS vector store

from langchain_community.vectorstores import FAISS
vectorstore = FAISS.from_documents(chunks, embedding_model)
  • FAISS = Facebook AI Similarity Search, the open-source vector library from Meta. (The transcript's "PyAS" / "Pius" is a transcription artifact — FAISS is the right name.)
  • In-memory by default. Stored objects are (id, vector, metadata, page_content).
  • Default distance metric is L2 (Euclidean). With normalized embeddings, L2 and cosine produce the same ordering. The score returned by similarity_search_with_score is therefore a distance — lower is better, not higher. That is why the lecturer's printed "score 32" for the top hit and "score 67" for a worse hit feels backwards if you assume higher-is-better.

Retrieval

retriever = vectorstore.as_retriever(search_kwargs={"k": 4})
results   = retriever.invoke("What is deep learning?")

# To see scores explicitly:
vectorstore.similarity_search_with_score("What is deep learning?", k=6)

The k=N argument forces N results to come back. If only 3 are genuinely relevant, you still get 7 weak ones. That is exactly what the reranker is for — to drop the weak ones based on a real precision signal.

THE LLM IS ALSO OPEN-SOURCE

The "Complete Guide" notebook uses google/flan-t5-small (~80 M params, seq2seq, ~300 MB download) via HuggingFacePipeline. The lecturer's reason was explicit: "I want you to try all of these things free of cost." For OpenAI or any commercial model you'd swap HuggingFacePipeline(...) for ChatOpenAI(model="...") — nothing else in the chain changes.

§ 08 — LCEL

The chain — and what RunnablePassthrough is really for

from langchain_core.runnables import RunnablePassthrough

rag_chain = (
    {"context": retriever | format_docs, "question": RunnablePassthrough()}
    | prompt
    | llm
    | StrOutputParser()
)

Several students got tangled up here. The cleanest way to read it: the dict {"context": ..., "question": ...} is the input contract for the next step (prompt). The prompt template has two placeholders: {context} and {question}. The dict says: to produce context, run the retriever over my input then format the docs; to produce question, just pass my input through unchanged.

RunnablePassthrough is just an identity runnable: input goes in, the same value comes out. It exists because in the LCEL dict-form, every value must be a runnable; you can't put a raw string variable there. RunnablePassthrough() is the no-op runnable you use to "forward the input as-is."

Correction worth flagging. The lecturer described RunnablePassthrough as related to parallel execution for many users at once. That's not what it does. The class that runs multiple runnables in parallel inside a chain is RunnableParallel — and even that is about composing branches of a chain graph, not about multi-tenant request concurrency. Concurrent users are handled by the application server (Spring Boot, FastAPI, etc.), not by anything in LCEL.
§ 09 — A POINT THAT CONFUSED THE ROOM

Prompt vs question

In this RAG chain both end up inside the LLM call, so the distinction blurs. The clean definition:

  • Prompt = a template. It is defined at design time, has placeholders, and lays out the instructions the LLM should follow (system message + structure + the slots {context} and {question}).
  • Question = the user's runtime input. It is substituted into one of the placeholders when the chain runs.
JAVA / SPRING BRIDGE

The prompt is a Thymeleaf / Mustache template file; the question is a request parameter bound into it. A prompt does not have to contain a question slot at all — system prompts that just define behavior ("You are a medical-coding assistant; produce JSON with these fields…") are still prompts.

The reason this RAG prompt has both {context} and {question} is that the LLM needs both: the retrieved chunks to ground its answer, and the question to know what's being asked. The two are kept separate in the chain graph because they come from different sources — context from the retriever pipeline, question from the runtime input.

§ 10 — RULES OF THUMB

Heuristics, honestly stated

  • "Reranker is compulsory." A strong default for prose-style corpora. For very small corpora (a handful of chunks) the recall-vs-precision distinction matters less. For latency-critical paths (<200 ms), even a small cross-encoder may be too slow.
  • "Hybrid is hit-and-trial." True. Run it both ways on a held-out set of queries and measure.
  • "Pick k large, then let the reranker drop." Reasonable. Common values: k=10 to k=30 candidates before reranking, top 3–5 after.
  • "Cross-encoder is slower but better." Almost always true on quality. Quantify your latency budget before committing.
  • "LLMs are probabilistic; even with a structured output parser the format is stable but the content isn't." Correct framing. The parser enforces the shape; the model still samples the content.

Glossary

Bi-encoder
Two-tower architecture (or one encoder applied twice) that produces independent vectors for the query and each document. Comparison is done after the fact with cosine / L2. Used by all vector retrievers.
Cross-encoder
Architecture where query and document are concatenated and fed through a single encoder. Outputs a scalar relevance score read from the [CLS] hidden state via a linear head. Used by rerankers.
Reranker
Second-stage model that re-scores the top-k candidates returned by a first-stage retriever. Almost always a cross-encoder in 2024–2026.
BM25
Lexical (keyword) ranking function. TF-IDF with term saturation and document-length normalization. From Robertson & Walker's Okapi system, 1995.
RRF (Reciprocal Rank Fusion)
Method for combining multiple ranked lists by summing 1 / (k + rank) across lists, where k is a smoothing constant (Cormack et al., SIGIR 2009). Default k=60 in LangChain's EnsembleRetriever.
[CLS] token
Special token prepended to BERT-family inputs. Its final hidden state is conventionally used as a pooled sentence/sequence representation for classification or scoring heads.
RunnablePassthrough
LCEL no-op that returns its input unchanged. Used inside chain dicts where every value must be a runnable. Not related to concurrency.
RunnableParallel
LCEL runnable that runs a mapping of runnables in parallel and returns a dict of results. About chain-graph composition, not multi-tenant request handling.
ContextualCompressionRetriever
LangChain wrapper that runs a base_retriever and then applies a base_compressor to shrink / re-score / re-rank the candidate list.
EnsembleRetriever
LangChain retriever that runs multiple retrievers and fuses their ranked lists via weighted RRF.
FAISS
Facebook AI Similarity Search, an in-memory vector library from Meta AI Research. Default L2 distance; lower-is-better when similarity_search_with_score reports a score.
BGE
BAAI General Embedding family of open-source embedding models from Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence. bge-small-en-v1.5 is 384-dim.
